Chapter 9.1

How can we describe wave motion?

Ropes, ripple tanks and springs will be used to help us explain how waves move through the world.


Learning Objectives

What you'll be able to do

  • Describe what is meant by wave motion, as shown by vibrations in ropes and springs.
  • Describe wave motion as shown by waves in a ripple tank, including use of the term wavefront.
  • Show an understanding that waves transfer energy without transferring matter.

Core concept
What a wave is

What is a wave?

Let's explore further into what waves are.

Learn
  • A wave is a disturbance or a vibration that transfers energy through a medium or space.Something wobbles. That wobble passes on to the next bit, and the next, and the next. Nothing is carried along. Think of a line of people in a stadium standing up and sitting down one after another. The Mexican wave crosses the whole stadium, but nobody walks anywhere.
  • A medium is the substance in which the wave travels, for example air, water or glass.The medium is just the stuff the wave goes through. For sound in this room, the medium is the air. For a wave on a rope, the medium is the rope. Light is the odd one out: it needs no medium at all.
  • Waves are produced by a disturbance or a vibration.
Key Facts
  • A wave transfers energy. It does not transfer matter.
  • A medium is the substance the wave travels in. Not every wave needs one: light travels through empty space.
  • The vibration is the cause. The wave is what spreads out from it.
Test

Which statement best describes what a wave does?

Core concept
Waves on a rope

Waves on a rope

Move one end perpendicular to the rope, over and over.

Learn
  • The wave travels towards the wall.The hump goes from your hand to the wall. That is the only thing that makes the journey.
  • Points P and Q vibrate perpendicular to the wave's direction, about their rest positions.Perpendicular means at right angles. The wave goes sideways along the rope, so P goes straight up and straight down. It always comes back to the same spot.
  • Energy in the kinetic store from the moving hand is transferred to the kinetic store of the rope and to the wall.Your arm is doing work. That energy goes into the moving rope, and the rope hands it on to the wall at the far end.
  • P and Q do not move from one end to the other end. This shows there is no transfer of matter along the rope.
Key Facts
  • The hand moves perpendicular to the rope, not along it.
  • Energy in the kinetic store is transferred along the rope.
  • P and Q staying put is the evidence that matter is not transferred.
Test

A paint mark is made on a rope. A wave is sent along the rope. What happens to the paint mark?

Core concept
Waves in a tank

Water waves in the tank

Each bit of water goes up and down. The pattern travels.

Learn
  • The waves move away from the dipper.Wherever you put the dipper, the waves head outward from it in every direction.
  • Water molecules vibrate perpendicular to the wave's direction, about their rest positions.Each bit of water goes up and down on the spot. The pattern moves sideways across the tank; the water does not.
  • Energy from the kinetic store from the dipper is transferred to the kinetic store of water.The motor shakes the dipper, the dipper shakes the water, and that shaking spreads.
  • The water molecules do not travel from one end to the other end. Again, this shows that matter is not transferred during energy transfer.
Key Facts
  • A spherical dipper generates circular waves. These lines are also called wavefronts.
  • A straight bar generates straight wavefronts instead.
  • Water molecules vibrate perpendicular to the direction the wave travels.
  • Matter is not transferred during energy transfer.
Test

In a ripple tank, a small piece of cork floats on the water while waves travel from left to right. What does the cork do?

Worked example
Waves in a tank

Practice: Example 1, the floating object

The marks are for saying the right two things, in the right way.

Example 10 / 6
1Think first, then reveal. Two steps ask before they tell.

In the set-up below, a rod is dipped into water to form water waves. Describe briefly the motion of the floating object as the waves move along the water. [2]

a rod dipping up and downwater waves travelling to the right2 marks
  1. Describe means say what happens. It does not ask why. It does ask you to be clear enough that someone could draw it.
  2. Two marks means two separate scoring points. One sentence that says the same thing twice earns one mark.
  3. It moves up and down (oscillates) about a fixed position.Saying it "moves" is not enough. The examiner wants the direction of the motion.
  4. It does not travel along with the wave, towards the far end of the tank.This is the point most answers miss, and it is the point the whole question exists to test.
  5. The wave transfers energy without transferring matter. The floating object is the visible proof.
  6. The floating object moves up and down about its rest position as each wave passes. It does not travel along the tank with the wave.Twenty-three words, two marks, nothing wasted.

Core concept
Waves on a spring

Waves on a spring

Fix one end of a spring, then push and pull the other end rapidly along a flat surface.

Learn
  • The waves move away from the hand.
  • Each coil vibrates parallel to the direction of the hand's motion.Parallel means in the same line. Here the hand pushes along the spring, so each coil shuffles forwards and backwards along the spring, not up and down.
  • Energy from the kinetic store of the hand is transferred to the kinetic store of the spring.Same story as the rope. Your hand does the work; the spring passes the energy on.
Key Facts
  • On a rope the vibration is perpendicular to the wave. On a spring pushed along its length it is parallel.
  • That single difference is what splits every wave into two types, which is the next lesson.
  • In both cases energy is transferred and matter is not.
Test

A spring lies on a bench with one end fixed. The free end is pushed and pulled rapidly along the spring's length. In which direction does each coil vibrate?

Pulling it together: three set-ups, one idea

All three carry energy along the medium, but each particle only oscillates about its own rest position.

✦Beyond the syllabusThe wave that crossed an ocean

Not examinable. Worth knowing anyway.

NOT EXAMINABLE 
The wave that crossed an ocean. In 1960 an earthquake off Chile sent a wave across the entire Pacific. It reached Japan twenty-two hours later, still carrying enough energy to wreck harbours 17,000 km from where it started. Not one drop of Chilean water arrived in Japan.
